topics.label: AI Literacy & Capability
topics.description: Critical capabilities needed to become AI fluent — frameworks, competencies, and workforce readiness.

articles.title: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review - Nature
articles.snippet: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focused on European public health contexts; competencies identified may differ from Australian healthcare settings and governance structures, though core digital literacy principles likely transfer.
takeaways: Map existing digital competency frameworks in your organisation against European standards to identify gaps in AI literacy specific to health roles.
Use the framework's competency domains to design targeted upskilling programs for staff at different levels (clinical, administrative, leadership) rather than one-size-fits-all AI training.

articles.title: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health - Frontiers
articles.snippet: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to focus on faculty development in public health education settings; generalisability to other sectors and non-academic contexts unclear without full article details.
takeaways: Faculty development programs can shift organisational culture from AI resistance to readiness; design interventions that address underlying concerns rather than just providing technical training.
In public health and other knowledge-intensive fields, upskilling educators themselves is a leverage point for scaling AI literacy across teams and organisations.
Targeted professional development for leaders and educators may be more cost-effective than broad workforce training in driving sustainable AI capability adoption.

articles.title: Bridging the AI skills gap: Preparing generation Z for the evolving job market landscape through innovative educational strategies - Sage Journals
articles.snippet: Bridging the AI skills gap: Preparing generation Z for the evolving job market landscape through innovative educational strategies  Sage Journals
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focuses on Generation Z and educational strategies, but geographic scope and specific educational contexts are not detailed in the snippet. Findings may apply broadly to developed economies with similar education systems, but implementation will vary by region and institution.
takeaways: Identify gaps between current Gen Z curriculum and emerging AI competencies needed in your industry, then design targeted upskilling programs that address specific technical and digital literacy deficits.

Incorporate 'innovative educational strategies' (e.g. experiential learning, cross-disciplinary projects, industry partnerships) into your employee development programs rather than relying solely on traditional training formats.

Start building AI literacy early in career pathways — waiting until employees are hired may be too late; collaborate with educational institutions to shape pipeline talent that arrives with foundational AI knowledge.

articles.title: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education - Nature
articles.snippet: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education  Nature
articles.generalisability: Limited — focuses on middle school education context; applicability to adult workplace AI literacy development unclear without seeing full methodology and geographic scope.
takeaways: Design AI literacy programmes using a holistic framework that integrates AI competencies with broader digital skills rather than teaching AI in isolation, which may improve transfer to real-world workplace contexts.

Identify which specific AI competencies (e.g. critical thinking about algorithms, data interpretation, ethical reasoning) are foundational and should be prioritized in literacy curricula before technical skills.

articles.title: Strategies for developing AI competencies in higher education - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Strategies for developing AI competencies in higher education  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Likely focused on higher education institutions globally, but generalisability to workplace AI literacy programs and non-academic organisational contexts may be limited without knowing the specific strategies reviewed.
takeaways: Identify which AI competency frameworks used in higher education (e.g., technical skills, ethical reasoning, domain application) could be adapted for employee upskilling programs in your organisation.

Consider how higher education's pedagogical approaches to AI literacy—such as interdisciplinary curricula or hands-on project-based learning—might translate into effective workplace training design for diverse skill levels.

articles.title: US Department of Labor promotes AI literacy across the American workforce - U.S. Department of Labor (.gov)
articles.snippet: US Department of Labor promotes AI literacy across the American workforce  U.S. Department of Labor (.gov)
articles.generalisability: US-specific — describes US Department of Labor initiatives, funding programmes, and policy frameworks that do not directly apply in Australia. Australian context requires separate investigation of local workforce development schemes and government support.
takeaways: The US DoL's approach emphasises partnerships between government, employers, and educational institutions to scale AI literacy — consider how similar cross-sector collaboration models might be adapted to Australian workforce development priorities.

US-specific: Federal funding and grant schemes mentioned are not available in Australia — check equivalent Australian Government initiatives (e.g., Skills Australia, state-based VET funding) for comparable support mechanisms.
Workforce-wide AI literacy is positioned as a national competitiveness issue — this framing may help justify investment in AI capability development programmes within your own organisation.

topics.label: AI & Organisational Psychology
topics.description: Impact of AI on wellbeing, engagement, job crafting, trust, and other org psych constructs.

articles.title: The effects of generative AI usage on employee knowledge behavior: a perspective based on the Automation–Augmentation Paradox - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The effects of generative AI usage on employee knowledge behavior: a perspective based on the Automation–Augmentation Paradox  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — theoretical framework paper that likely draws on existing research but may not include primary empirical data; applicability depends on how well the Automation–Augmentation Paradox framework generalises across different organisational contexts, sectors, and geographic regions.
takeaways: Generative AI presents a dual risk: it can either automate away employees' knowledge-building activities (reducing skill development) or augment their capabilities (enhancing learning). Managers should deliberately design AI usage policies that reinforce augmentation over pure automation to preserve employee expertise growth.

Monitor for 'knowledge atrophy' — the unintended consequence where AI handles routine tasks so completely that employees stop engaging in the deliberate practice needed to maintain and develop domain expertise. Create structured opportunities for employees to remain intellectually engaged with their work.

articles.title: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership - Nature
articles.snippet: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership  Nature
articles.generalisability: Limited — findings relate specifically to paternalistic leadership contexts, which are more prevalent in Asian organisational cultures. Applicability to Western/egalitarian leadership models unclear; requires validation across different leadership styles and cultural contexts.
takeaways: Foster psychological ownership of AI tools by giving employees meaningful input into how AI systems are configured and used in their roles — this increases collaboration and reduces resistance.

Paternalistic leaders can leverage their relational authority to encourage 'AI crafting' (customising AI use), but ensure this approach is culturally appropriate for your organisation's leadership philosophy and doesn't undermine autonomy.

Design AI implementations that allow employees to shape how the technology fits their work, rather than imposing one-size-fits-all solutions — ownership leads to better adoption and collaborative outcomes.

articles.title: The impact of artificial intelligence application on employees' job insecurity: the moderating roles of self-efficacy and transformational leadership - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The impact of artificial intelligence application on employees' job insecurity: the moderating roles of self-efficacy and transformational leadership  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample characteristics not revealed in snippet. The moderating variables (self-efficacy and transformational leadership) are likely relevant across sectors and geographies, but specific population, industry, and country details are needed to assess how widely findings apply.
takeaways: Build employee self-efficacy through targeted skill development and confidence-building interventions — this can buffer against job insecurity when AI is introduced, offering a practical lever beyond communication alone.

Transformational leaders who articulate a compelling vision and provide individualised support are better positioned to mitigate negative psychological impacts of AI adoption; invest in leadership capability development alongside AI rollout.

When implementing AI, simultaneously address both structural factors (the technology itself) and psychological factors (employee confidence and leadership quality) — tackling only one leaves employees vulnerable to insecurity.

articles.title: “Under the Shadow of Uncertainty”: the mediating role of job stress and the AI self-efficacy as a shield in cybersecurity behavior | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: “Under the Shadow of Uncertainty”: the mediating role of job stress and the AI self-efficacy as a shield in cybersecurity behavior | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Scope unclear from snippet alone — geographic location, sample size, and sector specifics not provided. Findings may be limited to cybersecurity professionals or specific organisational contexts; applicability to broader AI capability development in Australian organisations uncertain without full methodology.
takeaways: Build AI self-efficacy as a psychological buffer: employees with stronger confidence in their AI abilities experience reduced negative effects of job stress on cybersecurity compliance, suggesting targeted AI upskilling programmes may improve both capability and psychological resilience.

Address job stress when implementing AI systems: the mediating role of stress suggests that change management and psychological safety during AI adoption are as important as technical training for ensuring secure and effective technology use.

articles.title: When artificial intelligence becomes a job resource: how psychological capital fuels innovation in algorithm-driven workplaces - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When artificial intelligence becomes a job resource: how psychological capital fuels innovation in algorithm-driven workplaces  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear without access to full methodology — sample composition, size, and geographic scope not evident from title and snippet alone. Findings on psychological capital and AI as job resources may vary significantly across sectors and organisational contexts.
takeaways: Develop psychological capital (hope, efficacy, resilience, optimism) among employees working alongside AI systems — teams with higher psychological capital are better positioned to leverage AI as an enabler rather than a threat.
Frame AI tools explicitly as job resources that expand capability rather than replace it; this framing supports innovation and reduces defensive attitudes toward algorithmic systems.

Create targeted interventions to build psychological capital in algorithm-driven roles — coaching, peer mentoring, and framing success stories can strengthen employee confidence and creative problem-solving when working with AI.

articles.title: Algorithmic anxiety: AI, work, and the evolving psychological contract in digital discourse - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Algorithmic anxiety: AI, work, and the evolving psychological contract in digital discourse  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to be a discourse analysis of digital conversations rather than a direct empirical study. Generalisability depends on which digital platforms and time periods were analysed; geographic scope is unclear.
takeaways: Employees' anxiety about AI is linked to perceived changes in the psychological contract (implicit expectations about job security, autonomy, and fairness); managers should proactively communicate how AI will be deployed to preserve trust and clarify how roles will evolve.

Monitor and respond to employee concerns expressed in digital forums and internal communications — these reveal emerging anxieties about algorithmic decision-making before they escalate into broader disengagement or retention risk.

Frame AI adoption as a renegotiation of the psychological contract rather than a unilateral change; involve employees in discussions about how AI affects their work, decision-making autonomy, and career development.

topics.label: Behavioural Change Frameworks
topics.description: Evidence-based frameworks for driving behaviour change — in the context of AI adoption and workforce transformation.

articles.title: How AI is Reshaping the Future of Work - Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.snippet: How AI is Reshaping the Future of Work  Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to be a Stanford business school perspective piece without specified empirical scope. Likely reflects US higher education context and may not capture sector-specific or geographic variations in AI adoption challenges.
takeaways: Identify which roles in your organisation are most vulnerable to AI displacement and prioritise upskilling conversations with affected employees before anxiety peaks.
Frame AI adoption as a tool-complementarity story rather than replacement narrative — help teams understand how their role will evolve, not disappear.
Establish clear communication about how your organisation's AI strategy affects different job categories, as ambiguity drives resistance and disengagement during workplace transitions.

articles.title: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet alone — geographic scope and sample characteristics are not evident. The theoretical framework (approach-avoidance) may apply broadly, but generalisability depends on whether the study included diverse sectors, organization sizes, and geographic regions.
takeaways: Monitor whether your employees are actively reshaping their roles in response to AI tools (approach behaviors like upskilling) versus withdrawing or avoiding AI-adjacent tasks — each requires different management interventions.
Design AI rollouts to clarify how the technology expands rather than eliminates roles; uncertainty about job security can trigger avoidance behaviors that reduce the benefits of AI adoption.

Use approach-avoidance framing in change communications — emphasize opportunities to reshape work (approach) rather than focusing primarily on displacement risks (avoidance) to encourage proactive adaptation.

articles.title: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG analysis draws on global client experience but lacks peer-reviewed validation; findings reflect consulting firm perspective and may reflect client base bias towards large enterprises.
takeaways: Frame AI adoption as primarily a workforce capability and culture challenge, not just a technology implementation—invest proportionally in reskilling, role redesign, and change management alongside technical rollout.

Assess your organisation's readiness across three dimensions: technical infrastructure, employee mindset/willingness to learn, and manager capability to lead teams through transition—gaps in any one will limit adoption velocity.

Design early-stage AI initiatives to visibly improve daily work (reducing tedious tasks, enabling faster decision-making) so employees experience tangible personal benefit; this drives discretionary effort and reduces resistance in later phases.

articles.title: Redefine AI upskilling as a change imperative - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: Redefine AI upskilling as a change imperative  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — based on McKinsey's consulting experience across multiple sectors and geographies, but specific case studies and client contexts not detailed in snippet.
takeaways: Frame AI upskilling as an organisational change initiative rather than a standalone training program — this shifts focus from individual skill acquisition to systemic capability building and cultural readiness.

Treat AI capability development as a strategic imperative tied to business transformation, requiring executive sponsorship and change management support alongside technical training to drive adoption and behaviour change.
Design upskilling interventions that address resistance and mindset shifts alongside skills — this increases the likelihood employees will actually apply new AI capabilities in their day-to-day work.

articles.title: Generative AI adoption and employee outcomes: a conservation of resources perspective on job crafting, career commitment, and the moderating role of liking of AI - Nature
articles.snippet: Generative AI adoption and employee outcomes: a conservation of resources perspective on job crafting, career commitment, and the moderating role of liking of AI  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — findings depend on the study's sample size and sector coverage, which are not evident from the title and snippet. The conservation of resources (COR) theoretical framework is well-established, but generalisability across industries and geographies requires access to full methodology.
takeaways: Employee attitudes toward AI ('liking of AI') significantly influence how they adapt to generative AI tools — organisations should invest in positive exposure and training to shift perceptions before adoption, not after.

Job crafting behaviours emerge as a mechanism through which employees manage resources during AI adoption — consider enabling autonomy and agency in how employees redesign their roles rather than imposing top-down AI integration.

Career commitment may be at risk during AI adoption if employees feel threatened; proactively communicate long-term career pathways and skill development opportunities to retain engagement and trust during transition.

articles.title: Inclusive algorithmic work design: the moderating role of DEI interventions and diversity-supportive culture in AI-driven workplace transformation - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Inclusive algorithmic work design: the moderating role of DEI interventions and diversity-supportive culture in AI-driven workplace transformation  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear without access to full paper — depends on sample size, sector, and geographic scope of the study. The framework appears conceptually applicable across organisations implementing AI, but empirical validation scope is unknown.
takeaways: Combine DEI interventions with algorithmic work design changes — diversity-supportive culture acts as a moderator that can enhance or undermine the effectiveness of AI implementation, so these must be aligned rather than treated separately.

Audit your organisation's existing diversity culture before deploying AI systems; weak diversity support may amplify algorithmic bias or reduce adoption among underrepresented groups, even if the technology itself is well-designed.

Use AI-driven workplace transformation as a lever to strengthen inclusive practices — intentional design of algorithms with DEI principles front-loaded is more effective than retrofitting inclusion after systems are live.

topics.label: Fascinating Psychology Research
topics.description: Surprising, counterintuitive, and delightful findings from personality and behaviour research — the kind of study you'd share at dinner.

articles.title: When personality meets surprise: individual differences in memory for unexpected events - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When personality meets surprise: individual differences in memory for unexpected events  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample characteristics not provided in snippet. Findings about personality-surprise-memory relationships may vary across cultural contexts and age groups.
takeaways: Some personality types are naturally better at remembering surprising or unexpected moments — meaning your personality traits shape not just how you react to shock, but what you actually retain from it.

This suggests why two people present at the same surprising event often walk away with wildly different memories: their personalities predispose them to encode and store unexpected information differently.

The finding bridges two usually separate domains (personality psychology and memory science), revealing that how 'surprising' something feels to you isn't just about the event — it's about who you are.

articles.title: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality - PsyPost
articles.snippet: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Unknown from snippet — full methodology details needed to assess generalisability across different wine review datasets and populations.
takeaways: Language choices in wine reviews—like descriptive vocabulary and emotional tone—can reveal personality traits, suggesting our everyday writing leaves subtle behavioral fingerprints.
AI can detect patterns in unstructured text (like reviews) that humans might miss, opening up new ways to study personality through natural behavior rather than surveys.
Wine tasting provides an unexpectedly rich window into personality—the gap between 'fruity' and 'it tastes good' might say more about you than you'd expect.

articles.title: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people - ScienceDaily
articles.snippet: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people  ScienceDaily
articles.generalisability: Limited — based on a single neuroscience study with unknown sample size and geographic origin; headline-driven reporting may oversimplify complex brain imaging findings.
takeaways: Brain imaging studies often reveal structural differences between clinical populations, but 'shocking' findings in headlines frequently reflect modest effect sizes that don't straightforwardly explain behaviour.

Psychopathy is a spectrum trait present to varying degrees in the general population, not a binary category — so even if brain scans show differences, they're unlikely to be a simple on-off distinction.

Neuroscience news stories thrive on sensationalism; the actual research is probably more nuanced than 'shocking difference' suggests, making the original paper worth checking if you're genuinely curious.

articles.title: Surprising link found between hyperthyroidism and dark personality traits - PsyPost
articles.snippet: Surprising link found between hyperthyroidism and dark personality traits  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Limited — headline appears to report on a single study; generalisability depends on sample size and methodology not evident from the snippet.
takeaways: A medical condition (hyperthyroidism) appears correlated with psychological traits like narcissism or psychopathy — a counterintuitive link that challenges assumptions about the purely psychological origins of dark personality traits.

The finding raises a fun question: could some personality differences we think are purely psychological actually have metabolic or endocrine roots? It's a reminder that mind and body are more intertwined than we often assume.

articles.title: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe - University of Cambridge
articles.snippet: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe  University of Cambridge
articles.generalisability: Likely high — cross-cultural research from a major university suggests findings apply broadly across diverse populations, though specific sample demographics and size are not detailed in the snippet.
takeaways: Your taste in music says something universal about your personality, not just your cultural background — a Cambridge study found personality-music links hold across countries.
This flips the assumption that musical preference is purely culturally determined; instead, there's a deep personality signature in what people choose to listen to, regardless of where they live.
It's a fascinating reminder that beneath cultural differences, humans may share fundamental psychological traits that shape surprisingly similar aesthetic choices.

articles.title: New relationships take a surprising physical toll on older adults - PsyPost
articles.snippet: New relationships take a surprising physical toll on older adults  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Limited — details on underlying research methodology, sample size, and geographic scope are not provided in the snippet.
takeaways: Starting a new relationship later in life triggers measurable physiological stress responses in older adults — a counterintuitive finding that suggests romantic excitement comes with real biological costs, not just emotional rewards.

The finding challenges the assumption that relationship benefits (companionship, emotional support) automatically outweigh adjustment challenges — the 'cost of new love' appears to be a real phenomenon worth understanding.

topics.label: Psychological Safety
topics.description: Research on psychological safety and its role in team learning, AI experimentation, and innovation.

articles.title: When artificial intelligence becomes a job resource: how psychological capital fuels innovation in algorithm-driven workplaces - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When artificial intelligence becomes a job resource: how psychological capital fuels innovation in algorithm-driven workplaces  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear — the snippet provides insufficient detail on sample size, geography, methodology, and sector focus. Full article review needed to assess how broadly findings apply to algorithm-driven workplaces.
takeaways: Build psychological capital (hope, efficacy, resilience, optimism) as a foundation for employees to view AI tools as enablers rather than threats, which may reduce anxiety and increase willingness to experiment with AI features.
Design AI implementation approaches that actively develop employee confidence and agency — not just technical training — to unlock innovation potential in algorithm-driven roles.
Monitor whether psychological safety is being maintained as AI becomes embedded in workflows; without it, even resource-rich AI tools may fail to drive the intended innovation.

articles.title: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2025 - PwC
articles.snippet: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2025  PwC
articles.generalisability: Moderate to high — PwC's global survey captures broad workforce sentiment, but findings may reflect responses from larger, more formal organisations and may not represent informal economy or smaller businesses. Geographic representation and industry distribution not specified in snippet.
takeaways: Assess your current state against workforce hopes and fears identified in the survey to understand which psychological safety threats are most salient to your employees — this can prioritise intervention design.

Use the survey's framing of employee hopes and fears as a foundation for focus groups or pulse surveys in your own organisation to understand context-specific safety concerns before designing change initiatives.

Monitor whether trends in the global survey (e.g., job insecurity, fear of AI displacement) align with your workforce's concerns; if misaligned, this may indicate your organisational culture is either protecting staff better or facing distinct challenges.

articles.title: Algorithmic inclusion? The role of AI-assisted inclusive leadership in shaping gendered outcomes in multicultural academic teams - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Algorithmic inclusion? The role of AI-assisted inclusive leadership in shaping gendered outcomes in multicultural academic teams  Frontiers
articles.sample: Academic teams (geographic scope not specified from snippet)
articles.generalisability: Limited — findings from academic sector may not generalise to other organisational contexts; geographic scope unclear from snippet provided.
takeaways: AI tools can support inclusive leadership practices by reducing unconscious bias in team decision-making, particularly around gender and cultural representation in diverse teams.

Leaders should monitor whether AI-assisted processes inadvertently create new inclusion gaps — algorithmic systems may amplify existing biases if training data or design reflects historical inequities.

Inclusive leadership supported by AI requires intentional oversight: the technology alone doesn't guarantee psychological safety; human leadership commitment to examining and addressing gendered and cultural outcomes remains essential.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Limited — sample geography and size not provided in snippet. Findings on AI adoption's link to depression via psychological safety may vary significantly across different organisational cultures, leadership styles, and national contexts.
takeaways: Leaders implementing AI systems must actively foster psychological safety—explicitly encouraging questions about AI decisions, acknowledging concerns about automation's impact on roles, and creating safe channels for employees to voice ethical worries—to buffer against depression and anxiety.

Ethical leadership is critical during AI adoption; transparent communication about how AI will be used, who it affects, and what safeguards exist can mitigate psychological harm by reducing uncertainty and perceived unfairness.

Monitor employee mental health (depression, anxiety) as a key outcome during and after AI rollouts, not just productivity metrics—use surveys or pulse checks to identify teams experiencing heightened psychological distress so targeted support can be deployed early.

articles.title: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG research typically draws on global client work and surveys, but specific sample characteristics, methodology, and geographic distribution are not detailed in the snippet provided.
takeaways: Create structured opportunities for all employees to speak up without fear of embarrassment or punishment—this reduces barriers for underrepresented groups who may be more hesitant to contribute in traditional hierarchies.

Measure psychological safety as a lever for equity and inclusion: organisations that invest in psychological safety see more diverse perspectives surfaced, leading to better decision-making and retention across demographic groups.

articles.title: Why Innovation Depends on Intellectual Honesty - MIT Sloan Management Review
articles.snippet: Why Innovation Depends on Intellectual Honesty  MIT Sloan Management Review
articles.generalisability: Medium — presents conceptual framework from MIT Sloan perspective, but lacks empirical data or specific organisational case studies to demonstrate breadth of applicability across different industries and cultural contexts.
takeaways: Create explicit norms that reward admitting uncertainty and challenging assumptions without fear of retaliation — intellectual honesty requires psychological safety where people can say 'I don't know' or 'that won't work' without career consequences.

Establish feedback loops where failed experiments and honest mistakes are treated as learning opportunities rather than performance failures, enabling teams to innovate faster by testing ideas openly rather than siloing concerns.

Model intellectual honesty visibly from leadership — when leaders publicly acknowledge gaps in their knowledge, change their minds based on evidence, or admit when a strategy didn't work, it signals that honest discourse is valued over protecting ego.
